list.listitem: Candida and lichen sclerosus are common causes of balanitis. C

Other causes of balanitis should be excluded by culture or blood tests when the onset is acute, or if vesicles or chancre is present. Biopsy should be ordered if symptoms persist more than a few weeks or skin lesions do not resolve. C
Lichen sclerosus may increase the risk of phimosis and penile cancer. B
Fungal balanitis is treated with topical or oral antifungals and control of blood sugar. B
Lichen sclerosus is treated with a potent topical corticosteroid cream, topical calcineurin inhibitor, or circumcision. B

background.definition: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis or clitoris, and is most commonly applied to men. It is characterized by redness, tenderness, and sensitivity of the glans. Balanitis may present as phimosis, an inability to retract the foreskin, or paraphimosis, a painful constiction of the glans penis by the foreskin. Balanoposthitis is inflammation of the foreskin or glans.

list.listitem: In a cross-sectional study of 398 adult dermatology patients, the frequency of balanitis was 2.3% of circumcised males and 12.5% of uncircumcised males.
Among diabetics, 35% of uncircumcised patients had balanitis compared with none who were circumcised.
At an STD clinic in Portugal, 26% of men had candida colonization and 18% balanitis.
Fungal infection, especially candida
Lichen sclerosus is a chronic lymphocytic mediated skin disease also known as balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO)
Bacterial infections including anaerobic infection, bacterial vaginosis, treponema pallidum
Viral infectious causes including human papilloma virus, herpes simplex
Chemical irritants including soaps and lubricants
Allergy either systemic or local especially to latex
Psoriasis, erythema multiforme or atopy
Penile cancer
Necrotizing granulomas
Trauma
The uncircumcised penis is thought to provide an environment that increases the likelihood of balanitis because of the lack of aeration, increase in moisture and deposition of oils and debris.
Infection, irritants, allergens, or autoimmune factors then produce an inflammatory reaction at the head of the penis.
Lichen sclerosus is a lymphocyte mediated skin disorder mainly affecting the genitourinary area with a median age of 10.6 years old.
Candidal balanitis, often associated with diabetes, especially if poorly controlled, is typically acute in onset and moist, and presents with fine scaling erosive erythematous lesions. C
Lichen sclerosus lymphocytic infiltrate is usually chronic and may lead to phimosis, it presents as smooth erythematous lesions. C

Culture is recommended for patients with acute onset of symptoms, atypical presentation, or vesicles. Dermoscopy may assist in the diagnosis. Biopsy is recommended for patients with inflammation lasting more than a few weeks. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually moist, wet prep and culture verify fungus, usually candida, more acute onset, often associated with poorly controlled blood glucose. Cottage chees-like structure on dermoscopy
Biopsy verifies lymphocytic infiltration, tends to be more chronic, smooth red lesions. Linear irregular white areas on dermoscopy
Biopsy verifies cancer, most commonly squamous cell cancer, more chronic. Glomerular vessels on dermoscopy
Prodrome of tingling, burning or itching. Small tense vesicles on an erythematous base
Chancre present red papule develops into a painless ulcer that heals within 4-8 weeks
Presents as reddish silvery maculopapules often similar lesions in other locations especially the extensor surfaces, and is more chronic. Diffuse dotted vessels on demoscopy
Red target lesions usually with similar lesions in other locations
Appears as isolated areas with purple background and gray-brow peppering

list.listitem: Suspect balanitis in the patient with phimosis, pain, inflammation, or skin lesions on the glans. Patients presenting with acute onset of balanitis are more likely to have infectious or allergic causes, while patients presenting with more chronic symptoms are more likely to have lichen sclerosus or penile cancer.
Diabetic patients are more likely to present with fungal balanitis usually caused by candida. It is typically acute in onset and moist, and presents with fine scaling erosive erythematous lesions.
Lichen sclerosus lymphocytic infiltrate is usually chronic and presents as smooth erythematous lesions. It may lead to phimosis.
Patients having unprotected sex or with new sexual partners may have herpes simplex infection or treponema infection.

Ask about use of condoms or lubricants. Patients using lubricants for intercourse may have sensitivity to the ingredients in the lubricant, and use of latex condoms may cause a local reaction in patients with latex allergy.
Consider blood glucose level in patients with fungal balanitis.
Order cultures in patients with acute onset of symptoms or atypical presentation. However, culture for candida in fungal balanitis is only 35% sensitive.
Order Tzanck smear or viral culture for herpes simplex in patients with painful prodrome or vesicles.
Dermoscopy is noninvasive and helps to differentiate causes of balanitits.
Test for syphilis in patients with a chancre or a history of chancre.

Cutaneous biopsy should be performed in patients who have symptoms lasting more than a few weeks or fail conservative treatment. Biopsy identifies lichen sclerosus, penile cancer, human papilloma virus, psoriasis, erythema multiforme.
Acetic acid combined with colposcopic evaluation can be used to direct biopsy site selection.
Reflectance confocal microscopic is an invivo imaging method used to differentiate lichen sclerosus from penile cancer, but is not widely used.
Suspect balanitis in the patient with phimosis, pain, inflammation, or skin lesions on the glans.
Consider use of dermascope.

Order cultures in patients with acute onset of symptoms, atypical presentation, or if painful vesicles are present; order RPR if chancre is present or there is a history of chancre. Biopsy if conservative treatments fail or if skin lesions persist more than a few weeks.
Empiric treatment is education on penile hygiene for nonspecific balanitis and oral or topical antifungal agents when fungal balanitis is suspected.
Biopsy proven lichen sclerosus should be treated with potent steroid creams, or pimecrolimus 1%, and monitored for response to therapy.
Circumcision or referral to urology should be considered for treatment failures, unhealing skin lesions, or urinary obstruction or voiding complications.
Fungal balanitis is treated with topical or oral antifungals, and control of blood sugar. B
Lichen sclerosus is treated with potent corticosteroid cream, topical calcineurin inhibitor, or circumcision. Circumcision may be avoided with use of topical corticosteroids. B
Specific treatment of other causes is directed by clinical and laboratory findings. C

Fungal balanitis may be treated with topical antifungals such as clotrimazole or oral antifungals such as fluconazole. An unblinded randomized trial of 157 men with candidal balanitis found no difference in cure rates between a single dose of oral 150 mg fluconazole or twice daily clotrimazole for 7 days. However, there were 9 recurrences in the fluconazole group and only 2 in the clotrimazole group.
In patients with candidal infections showing resistance to azoles and terbinafine itraconazole, voriconizol or clotimazole may be considered.

Lichen sclerosus may be treated with potent steroid creams such as tramcinalone 0.5% or mometasone cream 0.1%. Clinical trials are lacking; a systematic review of 6 case series with 89 patients found that circumcision could be avoided after a median 20 months of topical steroids.
Optional treatment for lichen sclerosus and nonspecific balanitis: twice daily application pimecrolimus 1% cream or 0.1% tacrolimus.
Limited studies recommend use of topical mupirocin 2% or oral thalidomide for resistant cases.
See chapters on herpes simplex and syphilis for information on treatment of those conditions.
Circumcision should be considered in patients with voiding difficulties, urinary obstruction, phimosis, or paraphimosis that does not resolve with conservative treatment.
Circumcision using a combination of CO2 laser and cyanoacrylate may be considered.
Lesions associated with BXO frequently resolve within 6 months of circumcision.
Penile dorsal slit or sleeve technique procedure may be used for balanitis or phimosis.
Foreskin preputioplasty and intralesional triamcinalone has shown good outcomes.
Recommend good penile hygiene, including gentle foreskin retraction and use of saline solution or soap and water during bathing.
Avoid any agents to which patient is sensitive.

Referral to urology is recommended in patients developing voiding complications, urinary obstruction, paraphimosis, if circumcision is required, for treatment failures, or if penile cancer is suspected.
Prognosis is generally good if treatment is started early. B
Late treatment can lead to phimosis, urinary obstruction, and penile cancer. B
Balanits xerotica obliterans (BXO) may lead to secondary phimosis in 52% of patients, and voiding complications or urinary obstruction may occur in 27% of patients when the meatus is involved. B
BXO is associated with penile cancer with a reported incidence of penile cancer in these patients of 2.6% to 5.8%. B
